name: AI Digital Marketing Strategies for Athletes
objectives: Given what you want in the next four weeks, write one SMART marketing goal, with all five SMART parts, including a number and a date

Given the group you want to reach, write a short audience profile of who they are, what they care about, where they spend time online and what makes them act, checked with two or three real people from that group
Given your audience profile, choose two channels where your audience already spends time, with a reason for each and age rules and privacy settings checked

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Setting a marketing goal
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write one SMART marketing goal for the next four weeks.
This lesson builds toward: Given what you want in the next four weeks, you will write one SMART marketing goal, with all five SMART parts, including a number and a date.
Marketing without a goal is just posting. Decide what you want in the next four weeks: get noticed by college coaches, fill a youth camp, grow an audience a brand would care about, or build a following for your future career.
Make it SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. "Get 15 sign-ups for my free summer shooting clinic by June 30" is SMART. "Get famous" is not.
An AI assistant can help sharpen it: "I'm a high school basketball player. Help me turn 'get more college coaches to see me' into a SMART goal for the next 4 weeks."
Step by step:
- Choose what you want in 4 weeks.
- Add a number.
- Add a date.
- Check it is realistic and matters to you.
Words to know:
- Marketing: getting the right people to know, like and trust you or what you offer.
- SMART goal: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
Try it now: Write one marketing goal for the next four weeks. Ask an AI assistant to make it SMART, then edit it so it is true and realistic for you.
You can now write a SMART marketing goal.

check.q: What does the M in SMART stand for?
check.why: SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

check.q: Your goal is "get more coaches to notice me". What do you add to make it SMART?
options: A number and a date, such as 5 coach replies by March 1
check.why: A SMART goal has a number and a date you can check.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Knowing your audience
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Describe the people you want to reach in one short profile.
This lesson builds toward: Given the group you want to reach, you will write a short audience profile of who they are, what they care about, where they spend time online and what makes them act, checked with two or three real people from that group.
Your audience is the specific group you want to reach. A college coach, a parent of a 10-year-old who wants camp, a local business owner and a fan of your sport all want different things.
Write a short audience profile: who they are, what they care about, where they spend time online, and what would make them take action. Example: "Parents of local kids aged 8 to 12, busy, care about safe and fun coaching, use Facebook groups and Instagram, sign up when they see real reviews."
AI can help you brainstorm what your audience cares about. Then check it by asking two or three real people from that group.
Step by step:
- Name the group.
- Write what they care about.
- Write where they spend time online.
- Write what makes them act.
- Check it with two or three real people.
Words to know:
- Audience: the specific people you want to reach.
- Audience profile: a short description of who they are and what they want.
Try it now: Write an audience profile for your goal. Ask an AI assistant: "What else might this audience care about?" Add one idea, then ask one real person from that group if it is right.
You can now write a short audience profile for your goal.

check.q: Which belongs in an audience profile?
options: Where the audience spends time online
check.why: The profile covers who they are, what they care about, where they spend time and what makes them act.

check.q: An AI assistant brainstormed what camp parents care about. What do you do next?
options: Ask two or three real camp parents if it is right
Ask the AI again until it agrees with you
check.why: Check AI ideas with real people from that group.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Choosing your channels
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick two channels where your audience already spends time.
This lesson builds toward: Given your audience profile, you will choose two channels where your audience already spends time, with a reason for each and age rules and privacy settings checked.
A channel is a place you reach people: Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, X, LinkedIn, Facebook groups, email, a website, or in person at games and community events.
Pick only two channels to start, based on your audience, not on what is trendy. College coaches often look at highlight videos and recruiting profiles plus email. Camp parents may use Facebook groups and local flyers. Brands look at how engaged your followers are.
Check the age rules for each platform, and set your accounts so you control who can contact you. If you are under 18, involve a parent or guardian.
Step by step:
- List where your audience spends time.
- Pick the two best matches.
- Check age rules and privacy settings.
- Write why you picked each channel.
Words to know:
- Channel: a place where you reach your audience, like a social app or email.
- Engagement: how people interact with your posts: likes, comments, shares, saves.
Try it now: Pick your two channels and write one sentence for each explaining why your audience is there. Check the privacy settings on each account.
You can now choose two channels that match your audience and set them up safely.

options: A place you reach people, such as Instagram, email or a website
check.why: Channels are the places where you reach your audience.

check.q: A new app is trending, but your audience of camp parents is in Facebook groups. What do you do?
options: Pick channels where your audience already is, like Facebook groups
check.why: Choose channels by audience, not by what is trendy.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Drafting a 4-week plan with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use an AI assistant to draft a 4-week posting plan and edit it.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free AI assistant, you will create a 4-week posting plan with an idea, format and call to action for each post, edited to fit your schedule and with no live location, home or school schedule shared.
Give an AI assistant your goal, audience profile and channels, and ask: "Make a 4-week plan with 3 posts per week across these two channels. For each post give the idea, the format (photo, short video, story, email) and a call to action. Put it in a table."
A call to action tells people what to do next: "Sign up at the link", "Watch my full highlights", "Email me for camp info". Every post that supports your goal should have one.
Edit the plan so it fits your training and school schedule. Never plan posts that show your exact location in real time, your home, or your school schedule to strangers.
Step by step:
- Paste your goal, audience profile and channels.
- Ask for a 4-week table: idea, format, call to action.
- Edit it to fit your schedule.
- Remove anything that shares your live location or home.
Words to know:
- Call to action: a clear next step you ask people to take.
- Content plan: a schedule of what you will post and when.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for your 4-week plan in a table. Edit at least three rows so they fit your real schedule and voice.
You can now draft and edit a 4-week marketing plan with AI.

check.q: What three things should each post in your plan table have?
options: Idea, format and call to action
check.why: The lesson asks for the idea, the format and a call to action for each post.

check.q: The AI plan includes a story showing you leaving your house each morning. What do you do?
options: Keep it; it shows your routine
Remove it because it shares your home and schedule
check.why: Never plan posts that show your home or live location to strangers.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Writing posts that sound like you, honestly
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn plan ideas into honest posts in your own voice, with disclosures where needed.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI-drafted caption, you will rewrite it as an honest post in your own voice with a clear disclosure when a brand gives you anything, with no claim you cannot prove and the disclosure easy to see with the post.
AI can write a first draft caption, but people follow athletes because they are real. Ask AI for three options, then rewrite the best one in your own words. Read it out loud: does it sound like you?
Be honest. Do not use fake stats, fake followers or claims you cannot back up. Coaches, brands and fans check.
If a business gives you money, free products or any other benefit to post, the FTC (the US agency that enforces advertising law) says you must make that clear, for example "Ad" or "Thanks to [brand] for the free gear", right with the post, not buried in hashtags. In videos, say it and show it on screen. College athletes may also need to report deals; ask your compliance office.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for three caption options.
- Rewrite the best one in your own words.
- Remove any claim you cannot prove.
- If there is any brand benefit, add a clear disclosure.
- Read it out loud before posting.
Words to know:
- Caption: the text that goes with a post.
- Disclosure: a clear statement that you were paid or given something to post.
Official sources:
- FTC: Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers
- NCAA: Name, Image and Likeness
Try it now: Take one post idea from your plan. Ask AI for three caption options, rewrite one in your voice, and read it out loud. If it involves any brand, add a clear disclosure.
You can now write honest posts in your own voice and disclose brand relationships clearly.

check.q: Which US agency enforces the rule to disclose paid or gifted posts?
check.why: The FTC enforces advertising law in the United States.

check.q: A local gym gives you a free month to post about it. Where do you put the disclosure?
options: In a comment a week later
Nowhere, because it was not cash
Right with the post, easy to see
check.why: Any benefit counts, and the disclosure must be clear with the post.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Measuring and adjusting
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Track three numbers each week and make one change based on them.
This lesson builds toward: After each week of posting, you will record three numbers tied to your goal and choose one change for next week, recorded weekly in a sheet, with the change decided by you.
Pick three numbers that connect to your goal. For a clinic: link clicks, sign-ups and comments asking questions. For recruiting: profile views, highlight video views and coach replies. Follower count alone can mislead.
Most social apps show these numbers in their insights or analytics area for professional or creator accounts. Record them in a sheet once a week.
Each week, ask: what worked best, and what will I change? You can paste your weekly numbers into an AI assistant and ask for one suggestion, then decide yourself.
Step by step:
- Choose three numbers tied to your goal.
- Record them weekly in a sheet.
- Find your best and worst post.
- Make one change for next week.
Words to know:
- Analytics: numbers that show how your posts and pages are doing.
- Vanity metric: a number that looks good but does not show progress toward your goal.
Try it now: Final task: put your goal, audience, channels, AI-drafted plan and three numbers on one page. Run week one, record the numbers, and write one change for week two.
You can now measure your marketing with three meaningful numbers and adjust each week.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds SMART goal The goal is vague, or has no number or date. One goal with all five SMART parts for the next four weeks. The goal links clearly to recruiting, NIL, a camp or a career step and is realistic for the athlete's schedule. Audience and channels No audience profile, or channels chosen by trend rather than audience. A short audience profile and two channels chosen because the audience is there, with age rules and privacy checked. The profile was checked with real people and the reasons for each channel cite what they said. 4-week posting plan Posts lack a format or call to action, or the plan shares location or home. A 4-week table with idea, format and call to action for each post, edited to fit the schedule and safe. Every call to action points to the goal and the plan balances both channels. Honest posts Captions read as copied AI text, include unproven claims, or lack a needed disclosure. Posts in the athlete's own voice, with no unproven claims and a clear disclosure for any brand benefit. Video disclosures are said and shown, and NIL reporting was checked with compliance where needed. Tracking and change Fewer than three numbers, or no change written for week two. Three goal-linked numbers recorded for week one and one change written for week two. The best and worst posts are named with the numbers that explain the change. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why can follower count alone mislead you?
options: It may not show whether people take the action your goal needs
check.why: Choose numbers tied to your goal, like sign-ups or coach replies.

check.q: Week one shows your videos got many more clicks than your photos. What do you do?
options: Make one change, such as more short videos next week
check.why: Make one change each week based on your numbers.
